newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin festival pays tribute to legendary Kim Novak.
newsitem.headline: Berlin festival pays tribute to legendary Kim Novak.

text.p: Film star Kim Novak, famed for her role in Alfred Hitchcock's classic thriller "Vertigo", was set to receive a lifetime achievement award on Friday at the 47th annual Berlin film festival.

Novak, one of Hollywood's biggest sex symbols during her heyday in the 1950s and 60s, was set to receive the festival's top "Golden Bear" award after a retrospective screening of a restored version of "Vertigo", organisers said.

Clad in black and sheltering behind a pair of large dark glasses, Novak, still blonde at 63, was mobbed by autograph hunters when she arrived at Berlin airport on Wednesday, and posed for dozens of flashing cameras and televison crews.
She was set to tour the city and enter her name in Berlin's golden book for honoured guests on Friday before attending the award ceremony, the festival organisers said.
The film festival -- Europe's second most prestigious after Cannes, which is held in May -- awards the "Golden Bear" prize for lifetime achievement in the film industry every year.
Last year the recipient was Jack Lemmon. Previous winners have been Sophia Loren, Gregory Peck, Alain Delon and directors Billy Wilder and Elia Kazan.

Novak, whose real name was Marilyn Pauline Novak, started her career in 1953 when, according to Hollywood legend, producer Harry Cohn spotted her and snatched her on her way to a screen test at Columbia Studios.
She earned the nickname "Miss Deep Freeze" because she used to do advertisements for refrigerators. The name stuck after she established her image as a temptress, icy but tantalising.
Cohn hired the inexperienced actress on a minimal salary and set about turning her into the successor to Hollywood's "goddess of love", Rita Hayworth.
A string of successes paved the way to fame, including "Vertigo" and "Bell, Book and Candle" in 1958 and "Strangers When We Meet" in 1960.
Renowned also for her off-screen affairs -- her lovers included Hollywood stars James Stewart, Kirk Douglas and Jack Lemmon -- Novak sealed her screen image as the cool, sexy but unattainable blonde.
Critics say her last truly great film was "Kiss me Stupid" in 1964, a sex farce by Billy Wilder where she played alongside singer/actor Dean Martin.
The film was so shocking in its sexual frankness at the time that a U.S. Roman Catholic group called the Legion of Decency campaigned to have it banned.
In later years, Novak became bitter about Cohn's claim that he had "created" her.
"Harry Cohn did not make me. But I also feel as though I am not completely self-made. I think it was a combination of things that made it possible," she was once quoted as saying.
